# Logistic Regression in Tidymodels

> "In God we trust, all others bring data." - W. Edwards Deming

The previous chapter introduced logistic regression with a single predictor. This chapter adds more predictors and uses `tidymodels` to fit, interpret, and test the model, make predictions from it, and evaluate those predictions. Most of the second half is about evaluation, because turning probabilities into decisions raises questions that do not come up with a quantitative response: which mistakes cost more, what threshold to use, and whether the predicted probabilities can be taken at face value.

## Multiple Logistic Regression

Simple logistic regression has one predictor. Multiple logistic regression has several, combined in the linear predictor just as in multiple linear regression.

For observation $i$, the model is

$$
\log\left(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\right)=\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta},
$$

where $\pi_i=P(Y_i=1)$ and $\eta_i$ is the linear predictor. Equivalently,

$$
E(Y_i)=\pi_i=
\frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta})}
{1+\exp(\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta})}.
$$

As with one predictor, the response function is bounded between 0 and 1. The predictors can be quantitative variables, indicators for categorical variables, transformations, or interaction terms, exactly as in multiple linear regression. The coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood.

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="What changes in multiple logistic regression?"}

The interpretation changes from a simple odds ratio to a *partial* odds ratio.

For a quantitative predictor, $\exp(\beta_j)$ is the factor by which the odds of $Y=1$ are multiplied for a one-unit increase in $x_j$, holding the other predictors fixed.

For an indicator predictor, $\exp(\beta_j)$ compares the odds for the group coded 1 with the odds for the reference group coded 0, holding the other predictors fixed.

:::

## Example Using Tidymodels

:::: {#exm-24_1 .example title="Disease outbreak data and predictors"}

In a health study of an epidemic outbreak of a disease spread by mosquitoes, individuals were randomly sampled within two sectors of a city. The response was coded

- $Y = 1$: disease present,
- $Y = 0$: disease not present.

The predictors are:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $X_1$ | Age |
| $X_2$ | Indicator for middle socioeconomic class |
| $X_3$ | Indicator for lower socioeconomic class |
| $X_4$ | Indicator for sector 2 |

Socioeconomic class is represented by two indicators:

| Class | $X_2$ | $X_3$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Upper | 0 | 0 |
| Middle | 1 | 0 |
| Lower | 0 | 1 |

Upper class is the reference group. City sector is represented by one indicator, with $X_4=0$ for sector 1 and $X_4=1$ for sector 2.

::::

:::: {#exm-24_2 .example title="Loading and exploring the disease outbreak data"}

We load the data, name the variables, and code the response as a factor. The levels are in the order `0`, `1`, so `glm()` models the probability of the second level, disease present. (The previous chapter discussed why the order matters.)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(GGally)

tidymodels_prefer()

disease_data <- read.table("CH14TA03.txt")

names(disease_data) <- c("id", "X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "Y")

disease_data <- disease_data |>
  mutate(Y = factor(Y, levels = c(0, 1)))

disease_data |>
  count(Y) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Y  n proportion
1 0 67  0.6836735
2 1 31  0.3163265
```


:::
:::


Of the 98 people, 31 (about 32%) had the disease. Keep that number in mind. A "model" that predicts no disease for everyone would be right about 68% of the time, and any real model has to do better than that.

A scatterplot matrix gives a quick look at the response and predictors.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggpairs(disease_data |> select(-id))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='Scatterplot matrix of the disease outbreak response and predictors.' width=576}
:::
:::


The scatterplot matrix is good for a broad scan, but with a binary response and three indicator predictors, most of its panels are hard to read. Targeted plots work better. The next two focus on age and on the indicator variables.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disease_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Y, y = X1, color = Y)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("0" = "#D55E00", "1" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(
    x = "Disease status",
    y = "Age",
    color = "Y",
    title = "Age by disease status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='Boxplot and jittered points showing age by disease status.' width=576}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disease_indicator_rates <- disease_data |>
  mutate(event = as.integer(as.character(Y))) |>
  select(event, X2, X3, X4) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = X2:X4,
    names_to = "predictor",
    values_to = "indicator_value"
  ) |>
  group_by(predictor, indicator_value) |>
  summarize(
    disease_rate = mean(event),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

disease_indicator_rates |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(indicator_value), y = disease_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), vjust = -0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Indicator value",
    y = "Observed disease rate",
    title = "Observed disease rate by indicator variable"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='Bar charts showing disease rate by indicator value for middle class, lower class, and sector 2.' width=576}
:::
:::


The diseased group is older on average, and the disease rate is much higher in sector 2 than in sector 1. The differences by class are smaller. These plots describe one predictor at a time; the model will describe each predictor's association after accounting for the others.

::::

### Is the Logit Linear in Age?

The model assumes the log-odds change linearly with age. With a quantitative response we would check linearity with a scatterplot, but a scatterplot of 0s and 1s against age shows very little. Instead, we group the observations by age, compute the proportion with the disease in each group, convert it to a logit, and plot that against the average age of the group. This is called an *empirical logit* plot. If the points fall near a straight line, a linear term in age is reasonable.

::: {#exm-24_emplogit .example title="Empirical logits by age group"}

We cut age into six groups of about equal size. The empirical logit adds 0.5 to the counts, $\log\left((y + 0.5)/(n - y + 0.5)\right)$, so that a group with no cases (or all cases) does not give an infinite logit.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
age_groups <- disease_data |>
  mutate(
    event = as.integer(as.character(Y)),
    age_group = ntile(X1, 6)
  ) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(
    mean_age = mean(X1),
    n = n(),
    cases = sum(event),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(empirical_logit = log((cases + 0.5) / (n - cases + 0.5)))

age_groups
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  age_group mean_age     n cases empirical_logit
      <int>    <dbl> <int> <int>           <dbl>
1         1     4.65    17     1          -2.40 
2         2    10.5     17     4          -1.10 
3         3    17.9     16     8           0

5         5    35.6     16     6          -0.480
6         6    59.2     16     8           0
```

:::

```{.r .cell-code}
age_only_fit <- glm(Y ~ X1, data = disease_data, family = binomial)

age_groups |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_age, y = empirical_logit)) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = coef(age_only_fit)[1],
    slope = coef(age_only_fit)[2],
    color = "#0072B2",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean age in group",
    y = "Empirical logit of disease",
    size = "n",
    title = "Empirical logits by age group",
    subtitle = "Blue line = fitted logit from a logistic regression on age alone"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='Empirical logits of disease for six age groups plotted against mean age, with a fitted straight line from a logistic regression on age.' width=576}
:::
:::


With only about 16 people per group, each empirical logit is noisy, so we are looking for a clear curve rather than small wiggles. The third group (8 cases out of 16) sits well above the line, but two or three cases fewer would put it on the line. The points rise with age without an obvious bend, so a linear term in age looks adequate. If the points had curved, we would try a transformation of age or a quadratic term, just as in linear regression.

:::

## Fitting and Interpreting the Model

:::: {#exm-24_3 .example title="Fitting a multiple logistic regression workflow"}

We set up the recipe, model, and workflow and fit them.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disease_recipe <- recipe(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4, data = disease_data)

disease_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm")

disease_workflow <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(disease_recipe) |>
  add_model(disease_model)

disease_fit <- disease_workflow |>
  fit(data = disease_data)

disease_fit |>
  tidy()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept)  -2.31      0.643     -3.60  0.000319
2 X1            0.0298    0.0135     2.20  0.0276  
3 X2            0.409     0.599      0.682 0.495   
4 X3           -0.305     0.604     -0.505 0.613   
5 X4            1.57      0.502      3.14  0.00169 
```


:::
:::


`tidy()` returns the estimated coefficients on the log-odds scale. Exponentiating them gives estimated odds ratios, and we can ask for confidence intervals on that scale too.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disease_fit |>
  tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  rename(
    odds_ratio = estimate,
    lower_95 = conf.low,
    upper_95 = conf.high
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 5 × 5
  term        odds_ratio lower_95 upper_95  p.value
  <chr>            <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept)     0.0990   0.0254    0.323 0.000319
2 X1              1.03     1.00      1.06  0.0276  
3 X2              1.50     0.464     4.96  0.495   
4 X3              0.737    0.220     2.42  0.613   
5 X4              4.83     1.85     13.4   0.00169 
```


:::
:::


From the fitted model:

- Each additional year of age multiplies the estimated odds of disease by about 1.03, holding class and sector fixed.
- Compared with upper class, middle class multiplies the estimated odds by about 1.50, holding age and sector fixed.
- Compared with upper class, lower class multiplies the estimated odds by about 0.74, holding age and sector fixed.
- Compared with sector 1, sector 2 multiplies the estimated odds by about 4.83, holding age and class fixed.

A year of age is a small unit. The odds ratio for 10 years is $\exp(10\hat\beta_1)$:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disease_fit |>
  tidy() |>
  filter(term == "X1") |>
  mutate(odds_ratio_10_years = exp(10 * estimate))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  term  estimate std.error statistic p.value odds_ratio_10_years
  <chr>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>               <dbl>
1 X1      0.0298    0.0135      2.20  0.0276                1.35
```


:::
:::


Ten more years of age multiplies the estimated odds by about 1.35, holding the other predictors fixed.

The confidence intervals for both class odds ratios contain 1, and they are wide: the data are consistent with middle class having anywhere from about half to about five times the odds of upper class. The intervals for age and sector do not contain 1.

These are associations estimated from an observational study, not causal effects. People in sector 2 may differ from people in sector 1 in ways the model does not include.

::::

### Testing Several Coefficients at Once

The $z$ statistics and $p$-values from `tidy()` are Wald tests of one coefficient at a time. Socioeconomic class is a single variable represented by two indicators, though, and the question "does class matter, after adjusting for age and sector?" is a test that both of its coefficients are zero.

In logistic regression the counterpart of the partial $F$ test is the *likelihood ratio test*, also called the drop-in-deviance test. We fit the full model and a reduced model without the terms being tested. If the reduced model is correct, the increase in deviance,
$$
G^2 = \text{Deviance}_{\text{reduced}} - \text{Deviance}_{\text{full}},
$$
has approximately a $\chi^2$ distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of coefficients dropped.

::: {#exm-24_lrt .example title="Likelihood ratio test for socioeconomic class"}

`anova()` compares two nested `glm` fits. We fit both models directly with `glm()`; the full model has exactly the same coefficients as the workflow fit.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
full_glm <- glm(Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4, data = disease_data, family = binomial)

all.equal(coef(full_glm), coef(extract_fit_engine(disease_fit)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
reduced_glm <- glm(Y ~ X1 + X4, data = disease_data, family = binomial)

anova(reduced_glm, full_glm, test = "LRT")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Analysis of Deviance Table

Model 1: Y ~ X1 + X4
Model 2: Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4
  Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)
1        95     102.26                     
2        93     101.05  2   1.2052   0.5474
```


:::
:::


It might seem simpler to use `extract_fit_engine(disease_fit)`, which pulls the `glm` object out of the workflow, as the full model. Don't. Inside a workflow, the response is renamed `..y`, and when `anova()` is given models with different response names, it silently drops all but the first and prints a sequential table for that one model alone. There is no error, only a warning that is easy to miss, and the output looks like a valid deviance table.

Removing the two class indicators increases the deviance by only about 1.2 on 2 degrees of freedom, with a $p$-value around 0.55. After adjusting for age and sector, the data give no evidence that disease odds differ by socioeconomic class.

The same idea tests one term at a time. `drop1()` compares the full model with each single-term deletion.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
drop1(full_glm, test = "LRT")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Single term deletions

Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4

<none>      101.05 111.05                    
X1      1   106.20 114.20  5.1495 0.023253 * 
X2      1   101.52 109.52  0.4669 0.494416   
X3      1   101.31 109.31  0.2560 0.612892   
X4      1   111.50 119.50 10.4481 0.001228 **
```

For each term, the likelihood ratio $p$-value is close to the Wald $p$-value from `tidy()`. They are not identical, and with small samples or large coefficients they can be quite different. When they disagree, the likelihood ratio test is generally the one to trust, for the reasons covered in the previous chapter.

:::

### Seeing the Model on the Probability Scale

Odds ratios are constant, but the model's consequences on the probability scale are easier to understand. A plot of fitted probabilities against one quantitative predictor, with separate curves for groups, shows them directly. These are sometimes called effect plots.

::: {#exm-24_effects .example title="Fitted probability of disease by age, class, and sector"}

We predict the probability of disease over a grid of ages for every combination of class and sector.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
class_lookup <- tibble(
  class = factor(c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower"),
                 levels = c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower")),
  X2 = c(0, 1, 0),
  X3 = c(0, 0, 1)
)

effect_grid <- expand_grid(
  X1 = seq(1, 75, by = 1),
  class_lookup,
  X4 = c(0, 1)
)

effect_grid <- effect_grid |>
  bind_cols(predict(disease_fit, new_data = effect_grid, type = "prob")) |>
  mutate(sector = if_else(X4 == 0, "Sector 1", "Sector 2"))

effect_grid |>
  ggplot(aes(x = X1, y = .pred_1, color = class)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Upper = "#0072B2", Middle = "#D55E00",
                                Lower = "#009E73")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Fitted P(disease)",
    color = "Class",
    title = "Fitted probability of disease"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-alt='Fitted probability of disease versus age, with one curve per socioeconomic class, in separate panels for sector 1 and sector 2; the sector 2 curves are much higher.' width=576}
:::
:::


Sector has the largest effect: at every age and class, the sector 2 curve is far above the sector 1 curve. The class curves are close together, consistent with the likelihood ratio test.

The plot also shows something the odds ratios hide. The sector odds ratio is the same, 4.83, at every age, but the *difference in probability* between the sectors is not. For a young upper-class person, the probability goes from about 10% in sector 1 to about 36% in sector 2; for a 60-year-old, from about 37% to 74%. In logistic regression, a model with no interaction terms still produces different probability differences in different groups.

The curves extend over the full age range for every group, but some combinations, such as older lower-class people in sector 1, may have few or no observations. Predictions for combinations that are rare in the data are extrapolations even when each predictor is within its own range.

:::

### Interactions

An interaction term lets the effect of one predictor depend on another. In logistic regression, the interaction is on the log-odds scale: with an age-by-sector interaction, the age odds ratio is different in the two sectors.

::: {#exm-24_interaction .example title="Does the age effect differ by sector?"}


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
interaction_glm <- glm(Y ~ X1 * X4 + X2 + X3,
                       data = disease_data, family = binomial)

tidy(interaction_glm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

2 X1            0.0475    0.0214     2.22  0.0261  
3 X4            2.41      0.937      2.58  0.00997 
4 X2            0.409     0.598      0.683 0.494   
5 X3           -0.366     0.609     -0.600 0.548   
6 X1:X4        -0.0297    0.0270    -1.10  0.271   
```


```
Model 2: Y ~ X1 * X4 + X2 + X3
```

The likelihood ratio test for the interaction has a $p$-value of about 0.27, so the data do not show that the age effect differs by sector, and we keep the model without the interaction. If we did keep it, $\exp(\hat\beta_{X1})$ would be the age odds ratio in sector 1 only, and the sector 2 age odds ratio would be $\exp(\hat\beta_{X1} + \hat\beta_{X1:X4})$. With an interaction in the model, a coefficient by itself no longer describes "the" effect of its predictor.

:::

### Adjusted and Unadjusted Odds Ratios

The sector odds ratio from a model with sector alone is not the same as the sector odds ratio adjusted for age and class.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bind_rows(
  glm(Y ~ X4, data = disease_data, family = binomial) |>
    tidy(exponentiate = TRUE) |>
    mutate(model = "Sector only"),
  full_glm |>
    tidy(exponentiate = TRUE) |>
    mutate(model = "Adjusted for age and class")
) |>
  filter(term == "X4") |>
  select(model, odds_ratio = estimate, std.error, p.value)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  model                      odds_ratio std.error  p.value
  <chr>                           <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Sector only                      5.72     0.473 0.000227
2 Adjusted for age and class       4.83     0.502 0.00169 
```


:::
:::


Part of the difference comes from confounding: if the two sectors have different age distributions, some of the unadjusted sector difference is really an age difference. In linear regression, that is the whole story, and if a predictor is unrelated to the others, adding it does not change their coefficients. Logistic regression has an extra wrinkle: odds ratios change when a predictor is added even if it is completely unrelated to the other predictors, as long as it is related to the response. This property is called *non-collapsibility*.

::: {#exm-24_noncollapse .example title="Adding an independent predictor changes the odds ratio"}

We simulate 100,000 observations with a binary predictor $x$ and a standard normal predictor $z$, generated independently, so $z$ is not a confounder of $x$. The true model is $\text{logit}(\pi) = -1 + 1\cdot x + \gamma z$, so the conditional odds ratio for $x$ is $e^1 \approx 2.72$ for every $\gamma$. We fit models with and without $z$ for several values of $\gamma$.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2401)

noncollapse <- tibble(gamma = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)) |>
  mutate(
    estimates = map(gamma, \(g) {
      sim <- tibble(
        x = rbinom(1e5, 1, 0.5),
        z = rnorm(1e5),
        y = rbinom(1e5, 1, plogis(-1 + x + g * z))
      )
      tibble(
        `Without z` = exp(coef(glm(y ~ x, data = sim, family = binomial))["x"]),
        `With z` = exp(coef(glm(y ~ x + z, data = sim, family = binomial))["x"]),
        cor_xz = cor(sim$x, sim$z)
      )
    })
  ) |>
  unnest(estimates)

noncollapse
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  gamma `Without z` `With z`    cor_xz
  <dbl>       <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1   0          2.73     2.73 -0.00554 
2   0.5        2.53     2.67 -0.000445
3   1          2.28     2.71 -0.00353 
4   1.5        2.03     2.66  0.00299 
5   2          1.85     2.81 -0.00436 
6   3          1.62     2.77  0.00261 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
noncollapse |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Without z`, `With z`), names_to = "model",
               values_to = "odds_ratio") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gamma, y = odds_ratio, color = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = exp(1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("With z" = "#0072B2", "Without z" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(
    x = expression(paste("Coefficient of z, ", gamma)),
    y = "Estimated odds ratio for x",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Odds ratio for x, with and without an independent predictor z",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = true conditional odds ratio, e = 2.72"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](24_Logistic2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-alt='Estimated odds ratio for x with and without z in the model, plotted against the strength of z; the adjusted odds ratio stays at 2.72 while the unadjusted odds ratio falls as z gets stronger.' width=576}
:::
:::


The correlation between $x$ and $z$ is essentially zero, yet leaving $z$ out of the model pulls the odds ratio for $x$ toward 1, and the stronger $z$ is, the more it is pulled. Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions: the odds ratio with $z$ compares people with the same $z$, and the one without $z$ compares groups averaged over $z$. Two lessons follow: an odds ratio always has to be reported along with what it was adjusted for, and odds ratios from studies that adjusted for different variables cannot be compared directly, even when the adjustment variables are unrelated to the predictor of interest.

:::

## Thresholds

The default threshold of 0.5 is not always the best one. If false negatives are costly, we can lower the threshold so that more people are classified as having the disease. If false positives are costly, we can raise it.

::: {#exm-24_6 .example title="Sweeping the classification threshold"}

Instead of trying a few thresholds, we compute sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy for every threshold from 0.05 to 0.95.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
threshold_metrics <- function(predictions, cutoff) {
  predictions |>
    mutate(.pred_threshold = factor(if_else(.pred_1 >= cutoff, "1", "0"),
                                    levels = c("0", "1"))) |>
    summarize(
      threshold = cutoff,
      true_positives = sum(Y == "1" & .pred_threshold == "1"),
      false_positives = sum(Y == "0" & .pred_threshold == "1"),
      true_negatives = sum(Y == "0" & .pred_threshold == "0"),
      false_negatives = sum(Y == "1" & .pred_threshold == "0")
    ) |>
    mutate(
      sensitivity = true_positives / (true_positives + false_negatives),
      specificity = true_negatives / (true_negatives + false_positives),
      accuracy = (true_positives + true_negatives) / nrow(predictions)
    )
}

threshold_sweep <- map(
  round(seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.01), 2),
  \(cutoff) threshold_metrics(disease_predictions, cutoff)
) |>
  list_rbind()

threshold_sweep |>
  filter(threshold %in% c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75)) |>
  select(threshold, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy)
```

Choosing the threshold that maximizes accuracy usually means accepting low sensitivity.

:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="The threshold should reflect the cost of mistakes"}

A 0.5 threshold treats false positives and false negatives as equally bad. That may not be reasonable.

In disease screening, a false negative (a sick person who is missed) may be much worse than a false positive (a healthy person sent for a follow-up test). Then a lower threshold makes sense, because it catches more true cases at the price of more false positives.

:::

If the predicted probabilities are accurate and a false negative costs $c_{FN}$ while a false positive costs $c_{FP}$, the expected cost of classifying a person as positive is $(1-\pi)c_{FP}$ and of classifying them as negative is $\pi\,c_{FN}$. Classifying as positive is cheaper when
$$
\pi > \frac{c_{FP}}{c_{FP} + c_{FN}}.
$$
With equal costs this gives the familiar 0.5. If false negatives cost five times as much as false positives, the threshold is $1/6 \approx 0.17$.

```{.r .cell-code}
  select(threshold, false_positives, false_negatives, total_cost)
```

## ROC Curves

A Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve shows how sensitivity and specificity trade off across all possible thresholds. It plots sensitivity (the true positive rate) against $1-\text{specificity}$ (the false positive rate). Each point on the curve is one threshold: a very high threshold classifies nobody as positive, which is the point (0, 0), and a very low threshold classifies everybody as positive, which is (1, 1).

The diagonal line is a classifier that assigns probabilities at random. A useful classifier has a curve that bows above the diagonal, and a perfect one goes straight up to the upper-left corner, where sensitivity and specificity are both 1.

### Area Under the Curve (AUC)

The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes the whole curve in one number:

- AUC = 1: perfect separation,
- AUC = 0.5: no better than random,
- AUC < 0.5: worse than random, which usually means the event class was coded backward.

AUC has a direct interpretation. Pick one person with the disease and one without, at random. The AUC is the probability that the model gives the person with the disease the higher predicted probability (counting ties as one half). This is why AUC is called a measure of *discrimination*: it measures how well the model ranks cases above non-cases.

### What AUC Does Not Measure

AUC depends only on the ranking of the predicted probabilities, not on their values. Any transformation that keeps the order of the probabilities leaves the ROC curve and the AUC unchanged, even if it makes the probabilities wildly wrong. A model can have a high AUC and still give probabilities that are systematically too high or too low.

Whether the predicted probabilities match the observed frequencies is called *calibration*. If a model is well calibrated, then among all the people it gives a probability of about 0.3, about 30% have the disease. A calibration plot groups the observations by predicted probability and plots the observed proportion in each group against the average predicted probability. A well-calibrated model has points near the line $y = x$.

The *Brier score* summarizes calibration and discrimination together. It is the mean squared difference between the predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome, $\frac{1}{n}\sum(\hat\pi_i - y_i)^2$. Smaller is better, and predicting the overall event rate for everyone gives a baseline of $\bar{y}(1 - \bar{y})$.

::: {#exm-24_calibration .example title="Same AUC, different calibration"}

We compare the model's predicted probabilities with a distorted version, $\hat\pi^3$. Cubing keeps the order of the probabilities but pushes them all toward 0.

### Predictive Values Depend on Prevalence

Sensitivity and specificity describe the model's behavior within the cases and within the non-cases. The predictive values also depend on how common the event is. By Bayes' theorem,
$$
\text{PPV} = \frac{\text{sens} \times p}{\text{sens} \times p + (1-\text{spec})(1-p)},
$$
where $p$ is the prevalence, the proportion of the population with the event.

::: {#exm-24_prevalence .example title="The same test in populations with different prevalence"}

Consider a classifier with sensitivity 0.90 and specificity 0.90, applied to populations where the disease is more or less common.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sens <- 0.90
spec <- 0.90

predictive_values <- function(prevalence) {
  tibble(
    prevalence = prevalence,
    PPV = sens * prevalence /
      (sens * prevalence + (1 - spec) * (1 - prevalence)),
    NPV = spec * (1 - prevalence) /
      (spec * (1 - prevalence) + (1 - sens) * prevalence)
  )
}

predictive_values(c(0.001, 0.01, 0.10, 0.32, 0.50))
```

## Train-Test Evaluation

All of the metrics so far were computed on the same data used to fit the model. That is fine for learning the mechanics but gives an optimistic estimate of how the model will do on new people. The validation methods from Chapter 22 apply to classification just as they do to regression.

:::: {#exm-24_9 .example title="Evaluating the disease model on a testing set"}

We make a stratified split so that the training and testing sets have about the same proportion of disease cases.

## Things to Watch Out For

::: {.callout-warning collapse="false" title="Common mistakes with logistic regression and classification"}

- Getting the event level wrong. `glm()` models the second factor level; `yardstick` treats the first level as the event unless `event_level = "second"` is set. A mistake swaps sensitivity with specificity and PPV with NPV, and turns an AUC of 0.8 into 0.2.
- Judging a model by accuracy alone. Compare it with the no-information rate, the proportion in the larger class (@exm-24_null).
- Using 0.5 as the threshold without thinking about the costs of the two kinds of error (@exm-24_7).
- Choosing the threshold on the test data. The threshold is a tuning parameter; choose it with training data or cross-validation.
- Treating AUC as a measure of whether the probabilities are right. AUC measures ranking only; check calibration too (@exm-24_calibration).
- Carrying PPV and NPV over to a population with a different prevalence (@exm-24_prevalence).
- Reporting an odds ratio without saying what it was adjusted for, or comparing odds ratios from models with different predictors (@exm-24_noncollapse).
- Interpreting the main-effect coefficient as "the" effect of a predictor that is in an interaction (@exm-24_interaction).
- Fitting too many predictors for the number of events. With 31 cases, this dataset supports only a few coefficients, and adding more invites the separation problems described in the previous chapter.
- Reading odds ratios from an observational study as causal effects.

:::

## Recap

This chapter fit, tested, and evaluated a multiple logistic regression model with `tidymodels`.

| Idea | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Multiple logistic regression | Logistic regression with more than one predictor. |
| Linear predictor | The logit-scale fitted value $\eta_i=\mathbf{x}_i^\prime\boldsymbol{\beta}$. |
| Partial odds ratio | The multiplicative change in odds for one predictor, holding the other predictors fixed. |
| Odds-ratio confidence interval | A range of plausible values for a population odds ratio, found by exponentiating the interval for $\beta_j$. |
| Reference group | The group with all of its indicator variables equal to 0. |
| Empirical logit plot | Logits of observed proportions in groups of a predictor, used to check linearity on the logit scale. |
| Likelihood ratio test | Compares nested models by the drop in deviance, with a $\chi^2$ reference distribution; the counterpart of the partial $F$ test. |
| Effect plot | Fitted probabilities plotted against a predictor, with separate curves for groups. |
| Interaction | A term that lets the odds ratio for one predictor depend on another. |
| Non-collapsibility | Odds ratios change when a predictor related to the response is added, even if it is unrelated to the other predictors. |
| Predicted probability | The fitted probability that an observation is in the event class. |
| Predicted class | The class assigned after applying a threshold to the predicted probability. |
| Confusion matrix | A table of predicted classes against observed classes. |
| False positive / false negative | Predicted event when there is none / predicted no event when there is one. |
| Sensitivity / specificity | The proportion of events / non-events classified correctly. |
| PPV / NPV | The proportion of predicted events / non-events that are correct; both depend on prevalence. |
| No-information rate | The accuracy of always predicting the larger class. |
| Threshold | The probability cutoff used to convert probabilities into classes. |
| Cost-based threshold | $c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})$, the threshold that minimizes expected cost when the probabilities are calibrated. |
| ROC curve | Sensitivity against false positive rate across all thresholds. |
| AUC | The probability that a random event gets a higher predicted probability than a random non-event. |
| Calibration | Agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates. |
| Brier score | The mean squared difference between predicted probabilities and 0/1 outcomes. |
| Event level | The class treated as the event when computing classification metrics. |
| In-sample evaluation | Evaluating predictions on the data used to fit the model; optimistic. |
| Train-test and cross-validation | Evaluating predictions on data not used to fit the model. |

2. What does it mean to interpret a coefficient while holding other predictors fixed?

3. Why is an indicator variable needed for middle socioeconomic class but not for upper socioeconomic class in this example?

16. A false negative costs 9 times as much as a false positive. If the probabilities are well calibrated, what threshold minimizes expected cost?

17. Why is choosing the threshold that minimizes cost on the training data optimistic?

18. What does an ROC curve show, and what are the points (0, 0) and (1, 1) on it?

19. Give the probability interpretation of AUC.

20. A colleague reports AUC = 0.22. What is the most likely explanation?

22. A test with sensitivity and specificity of 0.90 is used to screen a population with 1% prevalence. Roughly what fraction of positive results are true positives?

24. Why should the odds-ratio interpretations in this chapter not automatically be interpreted causally?

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

1. It puts several predictors in the linear predictor. The model still uses a logit link, and $\eta_i$ can include quantitative predictors, indicators, interactions, or transformations.

2. The odds ratio for one predictor describes its association with the odds of the event when the other predictors are kept at the same values.

3. Upper class is the reference group. With three classes, two indicators are enough; when both are 0, the person is upper class.

4. It groups observations by the predictor, converts each group's observed proportion to a logit, and plots the logits against the group means. A plot of 0s and 1s shows almost nothing about the shape of the relationship, while the empirical logits show whether the log-odds change linearly with the predictor.

5. $\exp(10 \times 0.0298) = \exp(0.298) \approx 1.35$.

6. Class is one variable represented by two indicators, so "class has no effect" means both coefficients are zero. The likelihood ratio (drop-in-deviance) test compares the model with and without both indicators, using a $\chi^2$ distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.

7. The same multiplicative change in odds corresponds to different changes in probability depending on where on the S-curve the starting probability is. Probabilities near 0 change little in absolute terms; probabilities near the middle change the most.

8. The odds ratio for a one-year increase in age in sector 1 (where $X_4 = 0$). In sector 2 it is $\exp(\hat\beta_{X1} + \hat\beta_{X1:X4})$.

9. Confounding: if sector is related to age or class, part of the unadjusted sector difference reflects those variables. Non-collapsibility: even predictors unrelated to sector change the sector odds ratio if they are related to the response.

10. Disease present, $Y = 1$. `yardstick` treats the first factor level as the event by default, and here the first level is `0`, so without `event_level = "second"`, sensitivity and specificity (and PPV and NPV) would be swapped.

11. `"raw"` returns the linear predictor on the logit scale, `"prob"` returns a probability column for each class, and `"class"` returns the predicted class using a 0.5 threshold.

12. A false positive is a person predicted to have the disease who does not. A false negative is a person predicted not to have it who does.

13. Sensitivity is the fraction of people with the disease who are predicted to have it. Specificity is the fraction without the disease who are predicted not to have it. PPV is the fraction of positive predictions that are correct, and NPV is the fraction of negative predictions that are correct.

14. 68% of the people do not have the disease, so predicting "no disease" for everyone already has accuracy 0.68. The model improves on that by only a few points, and its sensitivity at 0.5 is low.

15. Lower the threshold to catch more true cases when false negatives are costly (higher sensitivity, lower specificity). Raise it to avoid false alarms when false positives are costly.

16. $c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN}) = 1/(1 + 9) = 0.10$.

17. The threshold was chosen to fit the particular errors in those data. Like any tuning parameter chosen and evaluated on the same data, it will look better than it will perform on new data.

18. It shows sensitivity against the false positive rate as the threshold varies. (0, 0) is a threshold so high that nothing is classified positive; (1, 1) is a threshold so low that everything is.

19. It is the probability that a randomly chosen person with the event gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly chosen person without it, with ties counted as one half.

20. The event level is probably reversed, so the metric is treating the probability of the non-event as the score for the event. Reversing it gives AUC = 0.78.

21. Yes. AUC depends only on the ranking of the predictions. One model's probabilities can match observed rates while the other's are systematically too high or too low; a calibration plot or the Brier score shows the difference.

22. $\text{PPV} = (0.9 \times 0.01)/(0.9 \times 0.01 + 0.1 \times 0.99) \approx 0.083$, so fewer than 1 in 10.

23. The model was fit to those same observations, so in-sample metrics are optimistic. A small testing set has few events, so metrics like sensitivity can change a lot with one or two observations; repeated cross-validation gives a steadier estimate.

24. The data are observational. Logistic regression estimates associations after adjusting for the included predictors, and people in different sectors or classes may differ in ways the model does not include. Causal conclusions need a stronger design or stronger assumptions.

<!--  \subsection*{Poisson Regression} -->


<!-- ## Introduction} -->

<!-- \marginpar{} -->
<!-- We consider now another nonlinear regression model where the response outcomes are -->
<!--                             discrete. -->





<!--                             Poisson regression is useful when the outcome is a count, with large-count outcomes -->
<!--                             being rare events. -->





<!--                             For instance, the number of times a household shops at a particular -->
<!--                             supermarket in a week is a count, with a large number of shopping trips to the store during -->
<!--                             the week being a rare event. A researcher may wish to study the relation between a family's -->
<!--                             number of shopping trips to the store during a particular week and the family's income, -->
<!--                             number of children, distance from the store, and some other explanatory variables. -->





<!--                             As another -->
<!--                             example, the relation between the number of hospitalizations of a member of a health -->
<!--                             maintenance organization during the past year and the member's age, income, and previous -->
<!--                             health status may be of interest. -->






<!--                             The Poisson distribution can be utilized for outcomes that are counts ($y_i = 0, 1,2, ...$ ), -->
<!--                             with a large count or frequency being a rare event. -->

<!-- ## The Poisson Distribution} -->


<!-- The Poisson probability distribution is -->
<!--                             $$ -->
<!--                             f(Y) = \frac{\mu^Y \exp(-\mu)}{Y!} -->
<!--                             $$ -->

<!--                             The mean and variance of a Poisson distribution are -->
<!--                             \begin{align*} -->
<!--                             E\{Y\} &= \mu\\ -->
<!--                             \sigma^2\{Y\} &=\mu -->
<!--                             \end{align*} -->


<!--                             Note that the variance is the same as the mean. -->


<!-- \marginpar{} -->


<!--                             Hence, if the number of store trips follows -->
<!--                             the Poisson distribution and the mean number of store trips for a family with three children -->
<!--                             is larger than the mean number of trips for a family with no children, the variances of the -->
<!--                             distributions of outcomes for the two families will also differ. -->

<!-- ## Poisson Regression} -->
